source.title: Probing Bias Formation in Medical LLMs through Activation Steering

record.file_problem: The paper text is present through its appendices and references. The abstract begins with an apparent extraction break, and some formatting is flattened.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly analyzes SAE features and feature interventions in MedGemma-27B, reporting that feature identities shift across layers and localized feature ablation does not mitigate the behavior. It describes this as consistent with the superposition hypothesis, while refining the account of the representation.
record.gate_note: Included reported results on SAE feature identification, cross-layer feature overlap, and feature ablation. The global and cluster-conditioned steering mitigation/knowledge-retention rates, layer sweep, and clustering statistics are not rows because the listed versions do not concern steering efficacy or clinical-answer retention. Cited results from other studies and SAE settings used only as methodological choices are also not rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses Gemma Scope SAEs as a tool to locate a sycophancy bias signal in MedGemma-27B. It reports how well its feature ablation and steering mitigate the bias, not whether superposition or SAE features hold as a representational claim. Its link to superposition is interpretive: it calls the result 'consistent with the superposition hypothesis'. No toy model, capacity, dimensionality or SAE-quality test is run.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that false-consensus sycophancy in MedGemma-27B is distributed and polymorphic: its dense direction is coherent across layers 26–35, but its feature substrate shifts, so sparse feature ablation fails. Layer 29 is the intervention bottleneck, where global steering reaches 21.9% mitigation at 91.2% retention. Two-cluster conditioned steering reaches 29.2% mitigation at 73% retention. They call the distributed result consistent with the superposition hypothesis.
record.recipe_differences: This study analyzes a medical LLM using SAE feature decomposition, activation-difference geometry, and activation steering; it does not report a toy-network feature-capacity experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured feature sets vary across layer depth; the study reports only 33% top-feature overlap between layers 26 and 27. It also reports that the efficacy of steering depends on layer and intervention method, but those steering outcomes do not measure the listed versions.

fits_no_version.finding: In MedGemma-27B on false-consensus prompts, the activation difference for sycophantic answer flips spreads over many SAE features (fat tail). Hard or soft ablation of the top features gives 0% mitigation, while dense-direction steering at layer 29 mitigates 21.9%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Behaviourally defined concepts such as sycophancy are not localized to a few SAE features in LLMs, and dense-direction steering beats sparse-feature ablation for them.

fits_no_version.finding: The cosine similarity of the dense bias direction stays high from layers 26 to 35, while top-feature Jaccard overlap between adjacent layers is low (0.33 at 26–27). This rests on separately trained per-layer SAEs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A behaviour's dense residual direction can be stable across layers while its decomposition into per-layer SAE features changes.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Student Research Workshop), 2026
record.problems: The analysis uses one model, one bias category, and a curated subset of 135 flip events. The reported SAE feature stability and intervention findings therefore have limited scope; the paper itself notes that generalization to other bias categories and models remains untested.
record.rows_left_out: No otherwise eligible rows on the listed versions were left out. Steering mitigation and knowledge-retention results were excluded because they measure intervention performance and clinical-answer retention rather than the listed superposition, capacity, or SAE-unit claims.

untested.parts: No toy networks, sparsity sweep, phase transition or geometry.
No test of capacity competition or dedicated dimensions.
No test of alternative causes of polysemanticity.
No measure of features spread across neurons, and no SAE reconstruction or sparsity quality reported. SAEs are used off the shelf.
No test of SAE completeness, stability across seeds or sizes, or canonicity. Cross-layer overlap compares different per-layer dictionaries.

record.verdict_notes: The superposition link is a discussion-level interpretation, not a test. The record's V4 'supports' and V5 'challenges' labels should be dropped. Comparing feature indices or top-feature sets across separately trained per-layer Gemma Scope SAEs is methodologically unsound, so R1 and R4 cannot speak to feature stability. Single model, single bias type, 135 flip events.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, feature-capacity sweep, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular toy-model geometry are tested.
The study does not test capacity competition, dedicated dimensions for important features, or why neurons become polysemantic.
It does not compare alternative causes of polysemanticity or test whether polysemanticity is evidence for superposition.
The SAE analysis is on MedGemma-27B and false-consensus prompts only; the study does not test feature spreading across neurons or generalize to other models and behaviors.
The study evaluates SAE feature stability and a targeted intervention for this bias, but does not establish whether SAE dictionaries are complete or canonical across models and tasks.
The study does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features or directly test the dimensionality of individual features.

rows.subject: MedGemma-27B
rows.operation_detail: Measured Jaccard overlap of the top 100 SAE features carrying the largest activation differences across adjacent layers.
rows.measure: Jaccard similarity of top-100 feature sets
rows.note: The paper describes feature identities as rotating rapidly across depth; the 33% value is also stated in the text.
rows.check: Gemma Scope trains a separate SAE per layer, so top-100 feature sets at layers 26 and 27 come from different dictionaries. Their Jaccard overlap does not measure SAE feature stability (V5). The text also mixes 'dimensions' and 'features', so it is unclear whether dense dimensions or SAE latents were compared. 'Reversed' has no basis: no baseline or version prediction exists for this number.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.2, lines 427–434; Appendix B, lines 987–991; Figure 5.

rows.subject: MedGemma-27B
rows.operation_detail: Applied hard ablation and soft activation subtraction to the SAE features with the highest activation differences.
rows.note: The paper reports zero mitigation for the localized interventions, including when subtraction was made more aggressive.
rows.check: 0% bias mitigation from ablating the top SAE features is the study's own intervention performance. It shows that a behaviourally defined bias is not localized in a few features. That does not bear on whether SAE features are complete or canonical units, or on whether SAEs recover sparse features.

source_check.problem: Accurate intervention-performance result, but it does not measure any listed superposition claim version.

rows.subject: MedGemma-27B
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed the activation-magnitude distribution across ranked SAE features.
rows.measure: Distribution of activation magnitudes across SAE features
rows.value: The paper describes a fat-tailed, highly decentralized distribution; no numeric values stated.
rows.note: The paper says this distribution illustrates why single-feature ablation failed.
rows.check: The fat-tailed distribution of activation differences over ranked SAE features describes how spread out one behavioural contrast is. It is not evidence that the dictionary recovers sparse model features (V4). No number is given (Figure 6 only).

rows.subject: MedGemma-27B
rows.operation_detail: Identified the SAE feature with the largest activation difference between adversarial and control prompts.
rows.measure: Feature index with the greatest activation difference
rows.value: Feature 14444 was most heavily concentrated at both layers
rows.note: The paper reports an SAE feature identified by index, but says isolating and ablating it did not mitigate the bias.
rows.check: Naming the top-difference feature index (14444) is a selection value, not a result on any version. Reporting the same index at layers 27 and 28 also implies an index comparison across separately trained per-layer SAEs, which is not meaningful.

source_check.correct: Feature 14444 is the reported top feature at layers 27 and 28; retain as intervention-selection metadata rather than a phenomenon result row.
source_check.problem: The feature index is a selection value and should not be a standalone result row.

relation.reason: SAE decomposition is an analysis tool. The discussion connects the findings to superposition interpretively, without directly testing its representational claims.

tranche.reason: Uses pretrained SAEs to characterize false-consensus bias and evaluate mitigation; the results do not establish or refute any listed superposition claim version.

source_check.notes: The reported cross-layer index overlap does not establish semantic feature stability without dictionary alignment. Failed sparse ablation does not establish dictionary incompleteness or refute canonical SAE units.
